title: Front-loop-only htr — FLO htr
subtitle: The taller single-loop variant — a softer ridge with more drape
excerpt: FLO htr inserts into the front loop only of each htr, leaving the back loop as a raised horizontal strand. Because the htr is taller than dc, the freed back loops create a more prominent ridge with a slightly softer drape — useful for textures where a dc ridge would be too dense.

glossaryTerms.definition: Half treble worked into the front loop only. Leaves the back loop free as a ridge. Produces a taller, slightly softer horizontal line than FLO dc — used where FLO dc would be too tight or dense.

heroPrompt: A crochet swatch in sage green DK yarn showing FLO htr rows, visible horizontal ridges with a softer, slightly airy texture compared to dc ribbing, close-up.

content.text: applies the front-loop-only technique to the half treble. Because htr is one step taller than dc, the freed back loops leave a slightly larger, looser ridge. The fabric has a little more drape than FLO dc ribbing and is a reasonable choice for shawl borders, lightweight garment edges, and any place where a gentler texture is wanted.
Work a foundation row of standard htr.
Ch 2, turn. Yarn over. Insert the hook into the front loop only of the first htr top.
Yarn over and draw up a loop (3 loops on hook). Yarn over and draw through all 3 loops.
Continue FLO htr across the row.

items.symptom: Fabric feels too loose or drapes more than expected
items.cause: Htr is naturally taller and more open than dc; FLO htr amplifies this
items.fix: Use a hook one size smaller to tighten up, or switch to FLO dc if the fabric needs to be firmer.

content.text: BLO htr is the reverse — ridge on the right side. The third-loop htr technique (camel stitch) works a completely different loop on the htr and produces a denser knit-like rib from the same stitch height.
